title: Palm oil and blood lipid-related markers of cardiovascular disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of dietary intervention trials
authors: Fattore E, Bosetti C, Brighenti F, Agostoni C, Fattore G
population: 51 dietary intervention trials in 49 articles to 30 May 2013, 2 to 16 weeks, comparing diets rich in palm oil, red palm oil, palm olein or sn-1,3 palmitic acid with diets rich in other fats; volunteers aged 16 to 70 years
funder: Supported by the Università Bocconi (Milan, Italy) and Soremartec Italia s.r.l. The funders had no role in the study design, implementation, analysis, or interpretation of the data.
authorConflicts: GF received funding for the submitted work, and CA and FB received funding in the previous 3 years and outside the submitted work, from Soremartec Italia s.r.l., described as a company that has a financial interest in products containing palm oil. EF received funding in the previous 3 years and outside the submitted work from the Associazione delle Industrie del Dolce e della Pasta Italiane.
result: Of the 51 trials, 19 were conducted with the support of the Malaysian Palm Oil Board, 12 with the support of private companies and 19 with the support of national or public research institutions; 1 did not state its funding. Against MUFA-rich diets, palm oil diets gave higher LDL cholesterol (weighted mean difference 10.75 mg/dL), total cholesterol, apolipoprotein B and HDL cholesterol; against myristic and lauric acid, lower total and HDL cholesterol and borderline lower LDL cholesterol (-4.70 mg/dL). Changes in total and LDL cholesterol were less evident in studies funded by the Malaysian Palm Oil Board than in those funded by other private or public institutions, and in Asian studies; these variables were closely related. Some evidence of publication bias for total and LDL cholesterol.
